1

Innovation strategy

Personalised nutrition is already possible today, although it is labour-intensive. The data exists, but decision-making is lacking. Appetune is an agent that tackles this problem. It translates the body’s signals into food choices and leaves the decision up to the individual.

The user communicates via various wearables such as a ring, watch or headphones and via a hologram. The phone app is merely the control centre. In a household with more than one person, the data is combined into a base meal, to which individual components are added for each person (Figure 1).

Appetune orchestrates the process, while partners such as Edeka, Picnic and restaurants supply the physical ingredients. In doing so, Appetune draws on Euromonitor’s ‘Rewired Wellness’ trend and McKinsey’s ‘Agentic AI’ tech trend in German grocery retail (Euromonitor International, 2025; Yee et al., 2025).

Appetune provides more energy and requires less effort in everyday life, with the long-term aim of achieving a healthier lifestyle.

Scenario techniques (T2) · Börjeson et al. (2006)

Predictive: We expect stable development in the key drivers: more people live alone and loneliness is widespread (Destatis, 2025; Krüger et al., 2024), health data is becoming part of everyday life (Bitkom, 2024), health is being approached preventatively (Euromonitor International, 2025; Pione et al., 2025) and infrastructure such as holograms and drone deliveries will grow. A key remaining question is how people will use agents for personal purposes.

Explorative: Two uncertainties remain: people’s trust in a platform for their bodily data (Bitkom, 2024) and whether daily life takes place at home or outside (HDE, 2026; PwC, 2025). This gives rise to the four scenarios shown in Figure 2.

Normative: Appetune is not waiting to see which scenario materialises but is selecting one and working towards it. The vision is the ‘Connected Market’ (Figure 3).

2

Customer need

The core need of both segments (Table 1), “I want to eat what’s good for my body without it taking any effort”, can be broken down into three levels:

  1. Functional: What you eat today without planning.
  2. Emotional: Reassurance that it is good for your body.
  3. Social: Not eating alone, but sharing meals at home or out and about.

The problem today is that the data is there, but the decisions are missing. Although wearables can measure sleep, weight and stress, they do not provide personalised nutritional advice. Nutritional advice is usually one-size-fits-all.

Personalising meals is recommended, as the same meals can trigger very different responses, yet these responses are predictable on an individual basis (Berry et al., 2020). Furthermore, personalised recommendations have a greater impact on dietary habits than general recommendations (Celis-Morales et al., 2017). Additionally, making changes at an early stage achieves the greatest benefits (Fadnes et al., 2022) and younger people today are adopting a preventative mindset (Pione et al., 2025).

An increasing number of people are living alone (Destatis, 2025) and loneliness is widespread, with 16% of people often feeling lonely, rising to 26% among those living alone (Krüger et al., 2024). This is why Appetune is designed to work not just at home alone. It also suggests market halls, canteens and restaurants, and plans meals for households.

3

Expected adoption

By 2050, two years after the nationwide launch, the target market will be Germany, covering both urban and rural areas. The basis is 33.4 million one- and two-person households projected for 2040 (Destatis, 2020), assumed stable until 2050 (range: 30–35 million). It is assumed that approximately 40% of these are aged between 20 and 50 and that 80% of them use wearables (Figure 4). The urban/rural population distribution is estimated to be 68:32 (Küpper, 2020).

Revenue will consist of subscription fees and a 5% commission on purchases made via partners. Online grocery shopping in Germany is driven mainly by perceived usefulness and trust (Gruntkowski & Martinez, 2022). Online sales of food and drugstore products currently have a market share of approximately 5% but are growing at double-digit rates (HDE, 2026).

The assumptions regarding the distribution of the tiers (Table 2; Figure 5) are conservative, as combining a subscription with data sharing creates a barrier (see Chapter 5). Data tier 0 lowers the barrier to entry, as users can start without providing body data, and Basic is the most affordable entry point. In rural areas, uptake will be lower due to less partner infrastructure and the recent introduction of drone delivery.

4

Feasibility

The technologies used are Agentic AI and wearables, which are already available in basic forms today and are expected to become standard by 2050. Agents’ acceptance depends on trust and perceived benefits (Zhao et al., 2025). Furthermore, the EU framework for body and wellness data (EHDS) has been in force since 2025 and applies stepwise until 2035 (European Parliament & Council of the European Union, 2025).

Economically, the product is ‘asset light’, as it has no dedicated market or fleet of its own, and revenue comes solely from subscriptions and commissions. Interfaces in 2050 are assumed to include holograms from wearables and kitchen appliances, as well as drone deliveries (Raghunatha et al., 2023; Frankfurt UAS, 2023; European Commission, 2023), treated as infrastructure, not further trends.

According to value mapping (Bocken et al., 2013), current value losses are due to food waste, primarily in private households (Umweltbundesamt, 2023), and unused wearable data. The potential value destroyed by data misuse is mitigated by data tiers and the principle that data remains with the user.

A new opportunity for value creation is predictable demand, leading to less food waste for supermarkets, producers and households (Kaipia et al., 2013).

Business ecosystems (T5)

Pidun et al. (2019) found that an ecosystem pays off only if all four of the following conditions are met and if every partner derives clear benefits (see Figure 6).

  • Malleable environment: agents, wearables and data rules are emerging right now.
  • Modularity: wearables, market, delivery and restaurants can be combined independently.
  • Need for coordination: no standards for body and dish data.
  • Strategic advantage: stores, logistics and kitchens come from partners.

5

Relative advantage

The closest alternatives in 2050 will be Big Tech companies offering delivery services (Scenario 1) or supermarkets and weekly markets (Scenario 4; Table 3). The main advantage of Appetune is that it offers personalisation based on a person's body rather than just their preferences.

Furthermore, unlike Big Tech platforms, Appetune is neutral, contains no advertising, does not favour its own products and works with all wearables, while ensuring that the user retains ownership of their data. Additionally, delivery services, market halls and restaurants are integrated into a single system that can be used by the entire household.

Although willingness to share wearable data with healthcare providers is high, data protection is the most common concern (Szeto et al., 2025). Keeping the data with the user addresses this concern directly.

Active innovation resistance (T7)

Joachim et al. (2018) found that people often actively reject innovations before trying them out. This is due to functional barriers (usability, value, risk) and psychological barriers (tradition, image).

That is why there is a specific design solution for every barrier (Table 4).

Functional · risk

“What happens to my data?”

Answer: There are three data tiers and the data stays with the user.

Functional · usage

“I don't want to shop differently.”

Answer: Supermarket and delivery stay familiar, so the agent only plans.

Functional · value

“Is the subscription worth it?”

Answer: The Basic tier serves as an entry point for testing purposes. There are benefits today and in the long run.

Psychological · tradition

“I eat what I want.”

Answer: The agent only suggests based on someone's vital signs, and the user decides or edits.

Psychological · image

“That's something for self-optimisers.”

Answer: Appetune focuses on energy, enjoyment and eating together instead of counting calories.

Evidence used. “Of n = 413 responses, 94% (n = 388) expressed willingness to share WAT [wearable activity tracker] data with a healthcare provider.” Section 3.3, Health Data Sharing, page 6. “[…] with privacy being the most common concern that was reported.” Section 4, Discussion, page 8.

Annotation. This survey shows a high willingness to share wearable data, with privacy as the most frequent concern. It supports the data-tier design and the trust argument in Chapter 5.

Reference. Umweltbundesamt. (2023, May 2). Essen für die Tonne? 11 Mio. Tonnen Lebensmittel landen im Abfall [Food for the bin? 11 million tonnes of food end up as waste]. https://www.umweltbundesamt.de/themen/essen-fuer-die-tonne-11-mio-tonnen-lebensmittel

Source type. Industry or institutional.

Evidence used. „Rund 11 Millionen Tonnen Lebensmittelabfälle sind im Jahr 2020 in Deutschland auf dem Müll gelandet.“ […] „Der mit Abstand größte Anteil mit rund 59 Prozent aller Lebensmittelabfälle (6,5 Millionen Tonnen) entstand allerdings in privaten Haushalten.“ [Around 11 million tonnes of food waste ended up in the bin in Germany in 2020. By far the largest share, around 59 per cent (6.5 million tonnes), arose in private households.] Introductory paragraph (first quote) and section “Wo entstehen die meisten Lebensmittelabfälle?” (second quote).

Annotation. These official figures from the German Environment Agency show that most food waste in Germany is created in private households. They support the value lost today in the value mapping in Chapter 4 and the waste argument in Chapter 5.

Reference. Yee, L., Chui, M., Roberts, R., & Smit, S. (2025, July). Technology trends outlook 2025 (5th ed.). McKinsey & Company. https://www.mckinsey.com/~/media/mckinsey/business%20functions/mckinsey%20digital/our%20insights/the%20top%20trends%20in%20tech%202025/mckinsey-technology-trends-outlook-2025.pdf

Source type. Course literature.

Reference. Zhao, X., You, W., Zheng, Z., Shi, S., Lu, Y., & Sun, L. (2025). How do consumers trust and accept AI agents? An extended theoretical framework and empirical evidence. Behavioral Sciences, 15(3), Article 337. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs15030337

Source type. Peer-reviewed academic.

Evidence used. “The results of this study indicate that affective trust, cognitive trust, and overall trust are all essential prerequisites for the user acceptance of AI agents.” Section 5.1 “Main Findings”, page 16.

Annotation. This empirical study shows that trust is the key condition for accepting AI agents, with perceived benefits building trust. It supports the feasibility argument in Chapter 4 and the decision to keep data with the user.
